en: Seeing him— tranquil, majestic, having accomplished his purpose, traveling alone as if with a multitude— someone on the road who followed the way of a mendicant, filled with wonder, spoke thus with palms joined in reverence:
Since you are unattached toward beings who are attached, and have conquered the horses of the senses while their horses remain uncontrolled,
I suspect, O one like the moon, that you are worthy of homage, being satiated by the supreme essence of wisdom.
O steadfast one, from the serenity of your countenance and the mastery you exercise here over your senses,
it is certain that you have accomplished your purpose, O bull-eyed sage; tell me, who was your teacher, from whom you attained this perfection?
He said to him: "I have no instructor; there is no one to be honored by me, nor anyone to be disregarded.
Know me to be self-existent in the Dharma, having attained Nirvana, incomparable with others."
Since that which was to be understood has been understood by me in its entirety— whereas it remained ununderstood by others— I am therefore called "Buddha.
Since the afflictions have been completely conquered by me, know me as a "Jina" (Victor).

And now, O gentle one, I am going to Vārāṇasī; there I shall beat the drum of the Deathless Dharma for the benefit of the world afflicted by sufferings— not out of pride, nor for the sake of fame or pleasure.
"Having crossed over, may I become one who ferries the world across; being liberated, may I liberate all beings.
Indeed, having beheld the world of living beings thus afflicted, this was my former vow.

What is surprising in this, that some person, having attained wealth, should restrain himself alone? But he who, having encountered a special opportunity, supports a great multitude with unblinking eyes— he is truly worthy.
For he who, standing on dry land, does not wish to rescue a man being swept away by the current is no man of virtuous character;
and he who, having found a treasure, does not provide for a poor person with wealth is unwise.
For it is fitting that one who is healthy should treat another struck by disease when medicine is at hand;
likewise, it is appropriate for one who has traversed the path to describe the way to one who has gone astray.
For just as a lamp produces light and yet does not become impassioned by it,
so too the Buddha produces the light consisting of knowledge and does not therefore become impassioned by it.
15.11 Just as fire is certainly present in wood, wind in the sky, and water in the earth,
so too is awakening inherent in sages, and the discourse on Dharma in the lands of the Gayas and the Kāśis.
"Ah, indeed! said Upagu, having saluted him; then, leaving him as he pleased, he departed. (The commentary notes:
"having spoken thus... having moved away").
Again and again, his eyes blossoming with wonder, he gazed upon the Buddha, his longing having been awakened.
Then the sage, looking about, gradually beheld the city of Kāśī, which resembled the city of Vasvokasāra.
Embracing both Bhāgīrathī and Vārāṇasī as they approached, like a friend, he clasped them in his arms.
Resounding with the songs of cuckoos in its groves of trees and frequented by great seers, he entered that very deer-park,
blazing with power and splendor like the sun at the beginning of the month of Vaiśākha.
Then there were those of the Kauṇḍinya clan and the one of great renown, as well as Bāṣpa, Aśvajit, Bhadra, and Jita;
[the reading *bāṣpo ’śvajid* is also supported by manuscript evidence].
Having observed him from afar, O monks, those five spoke these words to one another:
"This mendicant Gautama approaches, a man of pleasure who has turned away from asceticism.
He must certainly not be approached nor saluted; for one who has broken his vow is not worthy of honor."
If he should ever desire to sit, let a seat indeed be offered to him;
for the noble ones do not fail to extend hospitality to anyone who has approached them.
Having made a formal agreement, those monks sat down, and the Buddha approached them;
yet, the more he drew near to them, the more they broke their promise.
Then one man took his garment, while another, having prostrated himself, held his bowl; yet another took his food.
One person offered him a seat and water for honoring, while two others likewise brought water for his feet.
In this manner, they all performed every kind of respectful service toward him with great devotion;
yet they did not abandon the practice of addressing him by his clan name. To them, the Blessed One, filled with compassion, spoke:
"O monks, do not address the Arhat—who is worthy of honor—with disrespect according to former ways.
Indeed, for me, honor and dishonor are equal; however, I turn you away from demerit."
Thus, he who would speak of the Buddha— who acts with equanimity toward all beings for the welfare of the world—
by name alone, is like one who harms his teacher; such a wicked person follows a doctrine of annihilation, just as a son might act toward his father.
Thus addressed by the great seer, the best of speakers, who was compassionate in nature,
they replied with slightly smiling faces, having fallen away from truth through delusion and a lack of conviction.
O Gautama, you did not perceive the truth by means of that supreme excellence of asceticism;
what reason could there be for you to perceive an object that is difficult to achieve while remaining established in pleasure?
When those monks thus did not have faith in the Tathāgata regarding the true nature of reality,
and when they understood the path to awakening to be something other than that, he, the knower of the path, spoke to them concerning the path.
Behold these two as faulty sides, paths not leading to the attainment of immortality: self-exhaustion, which is resorted to by the foolish, and likewise attachment to the objects of the senses.
For when the mind is agitated by bodily hardships known as "austerities" and is thus oppressed,
one will never even find the common perception of the world, let alone the path of reality that transcends the senses.
For just as the darkness of night does not come to an end here by means of water-sprinklings but by a lamp,
even so the darkness of ignorance goes to its destruction by the fire of knowledge, and not by bodily austerities.
Just as one who desires fire does not obtain it by merely splitting and cleaving wood,
but obtains it by churning that very wood through the application of the proper means, so too does one attain the deathless state through yoga, and not through mere exhaustion.
He was not attached even to desires that lead to misfortune, for his mind was overwhelmed by passion and ignorance;
he was capable of attaining success even in the management of worldly affairs, let alone in the contrary practice of detachment.
For just as there is no medical treatment for a person struck by disease who eats unwholesome food,
so too, for one struck by the disease of ignorance and attached to sensual pleasures, how can there be peace?
Just as there is no peace for a fire fanned by the wind when it rests upon dry fuel,
so too there is no peace for a mind following after passion when it rests upon the objects of desire.
Having avoided these two extremes, he has prescribed for me another path by way of the middle;
it leads to the ultimate cessation of suffering, and is secure, auspicious, and free from ailment.
He was radiant with the splendor of the sun of true vision, borne upon the chariot of pure resolve;
he dwelt in the practice of right speech and delighted in the assembly groves of virtuous deeds.
He possessed a great abundance of blameless livelihood, was followed by the powerful escort of right application,
was everywhere protected by the guard of right mindfulness, and had the ground of concentration as his bed, seat, and dwelling place.
Thus, this supreme eightfold path is the means for carrying one beyond death, old age, and disease;
having fulfilled all that was to be done, such a person does not go again to either the next world or this one.
Having understood that "this entire suffering, its cause, its cessation, and the path itself [are thus],"— *Buddhacarita* 15.37.
Thus, when the injunction for the Dharma was heard, an unprecedented eye arose within me for liberation.
Birth, old age, disease, and likewise death; separation from the beloved, union with the unpleasant,
and the failure to obtain the desired object— this manifold suffering one undergoes.
Whether one is devoted to desire or has conquered the self, whether embodied or disembodied,
whatever activity is devoid of the [three] qualities (guṇas) is, in brief, associated with suffering.
For just as a fire, even if its flames are extinguished and it is but a small spark, does not abandon its innate quality of heat; so too,
even when the notion of self is stilled and rendered subtle, it remains certain to me that its very nature is suffering.
But the various defects such as passion, and the actions arising from those defects,
are the certain cause of suffering, just as water is the cause of a sprout.
In the continuity of existence, whether in heaven or below, the host of defects such as passion and the like is indeed the cause;
likewise, various actions are the cause for the diversity of inferior, middling, and superior states in each respective case.
Through the destruction of defects, there is no continuity of existence; and through the destruction of karma, there is no suffering.
For that object which arises from what exists does not arise again from what has ceased to exist.
O mind, that which is without birth, old age, or death; where there is no fire, no earth, no water, no space, and no wind;
which is without beginning, middle, or end; noble, unassailable, imperishable, auspicious—that is cessation.
The eightfold path that has been prescribed is the means for its realization, and no other.
Because they do not see this path, people wander about in exactly the same way as their own brothers.
In that very place, *Buddhacarita* 15.46:
"This suffering is to be fully understood; its cause is to be abandoned; and its cessation is likewise to be realized."
My mind has thus turned toward this path as something that must likewise be cultivated.

"Suffering has been fully understood by me; likewise, its cause has been abandoned, its cessation realized, and this path leading to it has been cultivated. Thus has the eye of insight arisen within me regarding these matters."
"As long as I had not seen these four noble truths in their true reality,
so long did I say, 'I am not yet liberated here,' nor did I perceive within myself that my purpose was fulfilled."
When I realized these truths, and having realized them, accomplished the purpose that was to be done,
then I declared, "I am liberated here," and I perceived within myself the fulfillment of my goal.
When the compassionate Great Seer had thus proclaimed the Dharma,
Kauṇḍinya of the Gotra attained the pure, stainless eye, as did hundreds of gods.
To him—tranquil, self-restrained, and one who had accomplished all that was to be done—the Omniscient One spoke, bellowing like a bull: "Have you understood?
The Great-souled One replied with these words: "I have well understood; I have grasped your supreme intention."
"Therefore, 'I have understood well'— with this as his title, Kauṇḍinya bore that clan-name in the world;
and he attained the status of seniority among the disciples of the Tathāgata, the supreme teacher, in the Dharma."
Hearing that sound, the yakṣas who dwell upon the mountains raised a great roar:
"Excellent! This wheel of Dharma has indeed been set in motion by one with supreme vision for the sake of leading all beings to the deathless."
With morality as its rim, tranquility and self-control as its felly, vast wisdom as its hub, modesty as its linchpin, and mindfulness, intelligence, fortitude, and vigor as its nave;
because of its profundity, truthfulness, and excellent teaching, it stands firm in the three worlds, irreversible by other doctrines.
Having perceived the sound from the *yakṣas* on the mountains, the hosts of gods in the sky raised that very clamor;
hearing it thus through the successive tiers of the heavens as high as the abode of Brahmā, the noise ascended upward.

And having heard from the great seer that the three worlds are unstable, some self-possessed inhabitants of heaven did not fall into passion for the various sense objects; through spiritual urgency, they attained peace even within the three worlds.
Thus, as soon as the Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion for the supreme welfare of the worlds, both in heaven and on earth,
water fell from the sky accompanied by a rain of flowers, and the inhabitants of the celestial realms beat their drums.

Buddhacarita 15.58 Then, having heard that the prince had gone forth from home, the king was overcome with grief and, overwhelmed by sorrow, spoke these words to his ministers: “Do you not see how my heart is rent asunder? For he, my son, has departed, leaving me behind. Alas! How can I endure this separation? He is my very life, my glory, and my hope for the lineage; he is my eye and my light. How shall I live without him?”
